experience.summary: Directing end-to-end flight software architecture, fault protection systems, and hardware-in-the-loop qualification for autonomous LEO Earth Observation smallsats and lunar transfer stages.
highlights: Architected and flight-qualified a memory-safe, zero-allocation flight executive in Rust (no_std) and FreeRTOS for dual-core ARM Cortex-M7 rad-tolerant flight computers across 3 orbital missions.

Engineered an autonomous hierarchical FDIR (Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery) subsystem, mitigating 98.4% of single-event upsets (SEU) and eliminating uncommanded safe-mode trips across 14 months of continuous on-orbit operations.
Directed end-to-end hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing and 72-hour thermal-vacuum 'Day-in-the-Life' acceptance campaigns, verifying 100% compliance with NASA Class D smallsat flight guidelines.
Formulated CCSDS 133.0-B-1 Space Packet Protocol telecommand decoders and high-throughput telemetry framers, achieving sustained 50 Mbps S-Band downlink with <0.001% packet loss.

experience.summary: Led attitude determination and control system (ADCS) flight software development, orbital propagators, and numerical simulation testbeds for autonomous rendezvous and rendezvous maneuvers.

Developed high-performance 6-DOF orbital propagation kernel in modern C++20 incorporating EGM96 geopotential harmonics up to 70x70, solar radiation pressure, and Jacchia-Roberts atmospheric drag.
Automated 100,000+ Monte Carlo trajectory dispersions leveraging NASA SPICE ephemeris kernels (NAIF DE440), accelerating launch window and conjunction risk assessments by 85x.
Authored spacecraft attitude control allocation algorithms for 3-axis reaction wheel momentum dumping via magnetorquer B-dot magnetic torquing.

experience.summary: Engineered real-time telemetry processing pipelines, low-level device drivers for avionics bus protocols, and automated ground station pass management software.

Implemented bare-metal C device drivers for CANopen and SpaceWire (ECSS-E-50-12C) bus controllers interfacing with optical imaging and multispectral payload instruments.
Built hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test harness emulating orbital dynamics and sensor noise to stress test flight computers prior to flight software burn-in.
Authored automated satellite pass scheduler and antenna pointing servomechanism control loops compliant with CCSDS SLE (Space Link Extension) standards.

experience.summary: Researched deterministic model-predictive guidance laws and autonomous relative navigation algorithms for miniaturized spacecraft operating in proximity to small celestial bodies.

Simulated onboard optical relative navigation algorithms in high-fidelity synthetic camera environments with varying illumination and albedo.
Co-authored technical recommendations incorporated into NASA Small Spacecraft Technology Program (SSTP) reliability guidelines.

blogs.title: Architecting Deterministic Flight Software in Rust on Dual-Core Cortex-M7
blogs.summary: A deep dive into zero-allocation memory architectures, Cortex-M7 MPU hardware task isolation, and how no_std Rust guarantees determinism in mission-critical satellite flight software.
blogs.content:
### 1. The SmallSat Embedded Dilemma

Modern CubeSats pack the avionics capabilities of legacy multi-ton spacecraft into the volume of a shoebox. However, radiation-induced bit flips, thermal oscillations from -40°C to +85°C in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), and tight power budgets turn software reliability into an absolute mission constraint.

Traditionally, flight software (FSW) has been authored in MISRA C or restrictive subsets of C++. While proven over decades, human-managed pointer arithmetic and manual memory bounds checking remain the single largest root cause of catastrophic safe-mode reboots in smallsat constellations.

In this article, we document our experience architecting and flying **AetherOS**, a memory-safe, deterministic flight executive running `#![no_std]` Rust on an ARM Cortex-M7 dual-core microcontroller (STM32H753XI) with radiation-mitigated packaging.

---

### 2. Zero-Allocation & Compile-Time Guarantees

In orbital flight software, **dynamic memory allocation (`malloc`, `free`) is strictly forbidden** during nominal operations. Heap fragmentation over an 18-month mission timeline can cause allocation failure during a critical station-keeping burn.

Using Rust without the standard library (`#![no_std]`), we enforce this guarantee at compile time:

```rust
#![no_std]

use cortex_m::asm;
use heapless::spsc::Queue;
use heapless::Vec;

// Statically allocated, lock-free ring buffer for CCSDS Space Packets
pub static mut TELEMETRY_QUEUE: Queue<TelemetryFrame, 64> = Queue::new();

#[repr(C, packed)]
pub struct TelemetryFrame {
    pub header: u32,
    pub timestamp_subsecond: u32,
    pub payload: [u8; 256],
    pub checksum_crc16: u16,
}
```

By leveraging `heapless` fixed-capacity structures, any routine that attempts an unbounded allocation simply fails compilation. Furthermore, Rust's borrow checker guarantees **data-race freedom between RTOS tasks** sharing sensor telemetry buffers.

---

### 3. Hardware MPU Task Isolation

While Rust prevents internal memory safety bugs, a single flight computer often hosts third-party scientific payload code that may be authored in C or Assembly. To protect the core Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) loop from payload crashes, we configure the Cortex-M7 **Memory Protection Unit (MPU)** into 8 discrete hardware privilege zones:

1. **Region 0 (Privileged Code):** Flash memory hosting FreeRTOS kernel and Rust core executive.
2. **Region 1 (Privileged SRAM):** Critical FDIR state flags and system telemetry ring buffers.
3. **Region 2 (Unprivileged Payload):** Isolated SRAM boundary assigned to experimental imager payload.
4. **Region 3 (Peripheral Registers):** Strictly mapped SPI and SpaceWire controllers.

When a payload task attempts an out-of-bounds read or write, the Cortex-M7 generates a `MemManage` hardware fault in under **42 nanoseconds**. The AetherOS fault handler captures the register state, isolates the task, and notifies ground control without disrupting orbital pointing.

---

### 4. Flight Heritage Results on Astraea-1

During Astraea-1's 20-month mission in 535 km Sun-Synchronous Orbit:
- **Total Telemetry Packets Transmitted:** 48,200,000+
- **Uncommanded Safe Mode Entries:** 0
- **Single Event Upsets Mitigated by FDIR:** 412 verified events
- **Average Task Jitter:** <68 microseconds (well below the 100 µs requirement)

Deterministic Rust is no longer an experimental curiosity for space systems—it is the modern standard for flight software reliability.

blogs.title: Implementing CCSDS Space Packet Protocol over Low-SNR S-Band Links
blogs.summary: Designing deterministic packet decommutators, COP-1 sliding window telecommand verification, and LDPC forward error correction frames for high-reliability smallsat downlinks.
blogs.content:
### 1. The CCSDS Standard in Modern Spaceflight

The Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) provides the international standard for spacecraft telemetry and telecommand formatting. The **Space Packet Protocol (CCSDS 133.0-B-1)** defines structured 6-byte packet headers that guarantee interoperability across NASA Deep Space Network (DSN), ESA Estrack, and commercial ground networks like KSAT and AWS Ground Station.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                   CCSDS Primary Header (6 Bytes)             |
+---------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
| Version (3 bits)    | Type (1 bit)      | Sec. Hdr Flag (1b)|
+---------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
| Application Process Identifier (APID) (11 bits)             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Sequence Flags (2b) | Packet Sequence Count (14 bits)       |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Packet Data Length (16 bits)                                |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

### 2. High-Throughput Packet Decommutation

When a satellite passes at 7.5 km/s overhead, downlinking telemetry at 50 Mbps over S-Band or X-Band, the ground station gateway must decommutate thousands of packets per second without memory bottlenecks.

Our open-source Golang telemetry gateway uses zero-copy slicing directly over binary buffers:

```go
type SpacePacketHeader struct {
    Version         uint8
    PacketType      uint8
    SecHdrPresent   bool
    APID            uint16
    SeqFlags        uint8
    PacketSeqCount  uint16
    PacketLength    uint16
}

func ParseHeader(buf []byte) (SpacePacketHeader, error) {
    if len(buf) < 6 {
        return SpacePacketHeader{}, io.ErrShortBuffer
    }
    
    b0 := buf[0]
    b1 := buf[1]
    b2 := buf[2]
    b3 := buf[3]
    b4 := buf[4]
    b5 := buf[5]
    
    return SpacePacketHeader{
        Version:        (b0 >> 5) & 0x07,
        PacketType:     (b0 >> 4) & 0x01,
        SecHdrPresent:  ((b0 >> 3) & 0x01) == 1,
        APID:           (uint16(b0&0x07) << 8) | uint16(b1),
        SeqFlags:       (b2 >> 6) & 0x03,
        PacketSeqCount: (uint16(b2&0x3F) << 8) | uint16(b3),
        PacketLength:   (uint16(b4) << 8) | uint16(b5),
    }, nil
}
```

---

### 3. COP-1 Command Verification Loop

For telecommand uplink, dropping a command or executing out-of-order instructions can endanger the vehicle. CCSDS Communications Operation Procedure-1 (COP-1) provides a sliding window frame retransmission protocol that verifies every uplinked byte before executing onboard actuators.
